projects.title: Spray N Pray
projects.shortDescription: Spray N' Pray is a fast-paced boomer shooter where you play as Justinian, a priest armed with dual revolvers. Dash, run, and jump through a demon-infested cathedral, vanquishing hellspawn and fallen angels to earn your righteous place in heaven.

mechanics.title: Advanced AI Systems
mechanics.description:
On Spray N Pray, I programmed an AI system featuring five unique enemy classes, each built to support varied combat scenarios and encourage strategic player movement.

Enemy Types

Grunt: Slow melee unit that closes distance and performs a heavy attack with long recovery.

Soldier: Ranged enemy that predicts player velocity for more accurate projectile attacks; swaps to melee up close.

Tank: Durable frontline. Uses lunge attacks to rapidly close distance and applies constant offensive pressure.

Flyer: Aerial enemy with ranged attacks, adding verticality to gameplay.

Bomber: Charges the player and detonates on contact, disrupting positioning.

Technical Breakdown

To implement these behaviors, I:

Built EQS queries to drive enemy positioning and attack distance logic.

Created a base enemy character + AI controller, which defines foundational behaviors including:
Death handling
Stun state machine

Developed individual behavior trees tailored to each enemy class to define how they evaluate threats, reposition, and select attacks.

This setup provided a scalable and reusable foundation, allowing each enemy type to behave distinctly while sharing core functionality.

Ultimately, watching players instantly understand and react differently to each enemy type was a highlight of the development process—and one of the most fun parts of the project to work on.

mechanics.title: Handling flying enemies in UE5
mechanics.description:
While working on enemy AI in Spray N Pray, I hit a limitation with Unreal's EQS: it only generates points on the NavMesh — great for ground AI, but not for flying characters. So I created a custom 3D EQS generator to solve the problem.

🔧 What I built:

A cube-shaped EQS generator that spawns points in 3D space around the flying enemy

Points are scored by distance to the player (closer = better)

Points are filtered out if:

They don't have a clear line of sight

They're too close to or overlapping with obstacles

The flying enemy moves to the best-scoring point

This process loops until it's close enough to the player

The core logic was implemented in C++, and the behavior is managed using Blueprint Behavior Trees — a flexible and powerful combo.

mechanics.title: Spawn System
mechanics.description:
I implemented a robust spawning and wave-management system that controlled how enemies entered the battlefield while supporting designer customization and playstyle variability.

Core Functionality
Dynamic Spawning Prototype

Subsystem triggered spawns based on an input enemy list

Enemy types used EQS queries to find ideal spawn locations

Allowed quick iteration but produced overly random pacing

Hand-Placed Spawn System

To ensure curated encounters, we transitioned to designer-placed spawn points:

Guaranteed consistent combat flow

Allowed specific control of pressure & movement

Made encounters easier to tune

This eliminated randomness and encouraged intentional room-by-room design.

Wave Logic Evolution

Next wave spawns when all enemies are defeated

Added a variable to define the minimum number of enemies remaining before triggering the next wave
→ Allowed smarter pacing during fast-kill scenarios

If a wave has a mini-boss, the next wave will only begin after it dies, regardless of other enemies
→ Supports set-piece encounters

Difficulty Scaling

To support replayability and challenge levels, I extended the system with difficulty-driven spawning:

Higher difficulties (Hard / Insane) pulled from different enemy spawn lists

Increased total enemy count per wave

Adjusted wave makeup to add tougher or additional units

This allowed difficulty to scale without requiring designers to modify level data.

Polish

Added Niagara particle VFX on enemy spawn to improve visual clarity & anticipation

Result

This system empowered designers to craft intentional combat scenarios, supported scalable difficulty, and maintained modularity through data-driven enemy lists. The end result was an encounter system that felt challenging, dynamic, and adaptable.

projects.title: Zerolock
projects.shortDescription: Zerolock is a hero-based, multiplayer third-person shooter inspired by Valve's Deadlock. The project is built in Unreal Engine with a strong focus on responsive online gameplay using the Gameplay Ability System (GAS) and Unreal's networking framework.

mechanics.title: Advanced Movement System
mechanics.description:
Recreating Advanced Player Movement from Deadlock in Unreal Engine 5 (Multiplayer Ready)
Inspired by the fluid and responsive movement mechanics in Deadlock by Valve, I undertook a personal project to replicate a similar system within Unreal Engine 5, implemented entirely in C++ with full multiplayer networking support.
The custom movement system includes dash, slide, mantle, wall bounce, and wall run.

This project allowed me to:
🔧 Analyze and translate complex movement mechanics into Unreal's framework
🔧 Implement efficient and responsive network replication for multiplayer gameplay
🔧 Refine my understanding of character physics, animation blending, and gameplay responsiveness

All movement features were developed from the ground up to closely match the feel of modern AAA movement systems, while maintaining performance and consistency across networked sessions.

mechanics.title: Gameplay Ability System

mechanics.title: ItemShop UI
mechanics.description:
Designing a scalable, data-driven Item Shop UI (Unreal Engine, C++)

I've been building the Item Shop system for my Deadlock-inspired project and wanted to share a breakdown of the UI architecture and design decisions behind it.

The focus was on modularity, separation of concerns, and data-driven behavior, while keeping the system easy to extend as the project grows.

### Base shop controller

The Item Shop is driven by a base shop widget that acts as the UI controller.

It contains:
- Three category selection buttons
- A CommonActivatableWidgetSwitcher to swap between categories

Category switching is handled entirely through the switcher, allowing the UI to transition cleanly without rebuilding widgets or duplicating logic. Each category exists as its own widget with a clearly defined responsibility.

### Data-driven population

The base shop widget reads from an Item DataTable, iterates through all entries, and:
- Determines the appropriate category for each item
- Routes the item to the correct category widget

This keeps item presentation fully data-driven and minimizes UI-side coupling.

### Tier-based organization

Each category widget contains four CommonTileViews, one per item tier.
Items are inserted into the appropriate TileView based on their tier, providing:
- Clear visual hierarchy
- Consistent layout rules
- Easy scalability as tiers or items change

### Entry widgets and tooltips

Each TileView uses a custom Entry Widget that:
- Receives item data
- Builds a CommonButtonBase
- Displays item visuals and core metadata

Detailed information is shown through a custom tooltip widget attached to each button, which appears on hover and keeps the main UI focused and uncluttered.

### Interaction & HUD integration

Item interactions (buy, sell, upgrade) are routed through a single interaction path, with gameplay logic kept separate from UI concerns.

On the HUD side, a dedicated Inventory Widget stores and displays all purchased items, ensuring the UI always reflects the player's actual game state.

This creates a clean flow:
**Shop → Purchase → Inventory → Gameplay**

The full project architecture demonstrates a clean, extensible approach to game UI systems that scales with project complexity while maintaining clear separation of concerns.

mechanics.title: ItemData
mechanics.description:
Automating a Data-Driven Item Pipeline in Unreal Engine (C++ / Python / Editor Tools)

For my project ZeroLock, I built an end-to-end item pipeline focused on scalability and minimizing manual content work.

### Data Ingestion

Pulled item names, descriptions, and images from an external API

Parsed the response via a Python script that reads JSON and automatically:
- Creates UPrimaryDataAsset items
- Assigns core metadata
- Places assets into structured folders by category

### Editor Tooling

Built an Editor Utility Widget to handle everything designers usually do by hand:
- Assign item type (Weapon / Spirit / Vitality)
- Assign tier (T1–T4)
- Batch-register items into:
  - Type-specific DataTables
  - A master DataTable containing all items

### Runtime Integration

Items are consumed by a replicated Inventory Component
- Buying/selling applies GameplayEffects and grants/removes abilities via GAS
- UI is fully data-driven and reacts to replicated inventory state

### The Result

✅ Zero manual asset setup after ingestion
✅ Consistent item data across systems
✅ Fast iteration when adding or rebalancing items
✅ A pipeline that scales cleanly as content grows

This architecture demonstrates how automation, data-driven design, and editor tooling can drastically reduce manual content work while maintaining flexibility and consistency across gameplay systems.

mechanics.title: MVVM-driven HUD architecture in Unreal
mechanics.description:
Recently finished building a fully MVVM-based HUD with a strict separation rule: UI has zero knowledge of gameplay systems. No direct references to the Character, Ability System Component, or Controller. Widgets are stateless, disposable skins that bind only to ViewModels. All widgets resolve their data through UE MVVM, with ViewModels created using a mix of Manual and Resolver-based creation methods, depending on ownership, lifetime, and context.

### ViewModel Creation Strategy

**Resolver-based creation**
- ViewModels are automatically resolved from Player or GameState context
- Allows widgets to discover data without knowing where it lives

**Manual creation**
- Used when ViewModels require explicit dependencies or controlled lifetime
- Most notable for dynamic UI like the Game Stats Bar, where entries are spawned as players join
- Keeps ownership explicit and prevents UI → gameplay coupling

### HUD Components

**Attribute-Driven UI (Health + Ammo)**
- Both components powered by the same Attribute ViewModel
- ViewModel listens to GAS attribute changes and exposes normalized, display-ready values
- No widget-side math, no direct ASC access
- Multiple widgets consume the same VM without duplicating logic

**Ability Bar**
- Represents the player's active abilities
- Each slot binds to its own Ability ViewModel
- GAS remains authoritative over activation and cooldowns
- ViewModel exposes cooldown state as observable values (0 → 1 progress, remaining time strings)
- UI reacts purely through bindings

**Game Stats Bar**
- Dynamically tracks players as they join or leave
- Resolves team affiliation via the GameState
- Displays player icon, name, and K / D / A
- Entirely driven by GameState → ViewModel propagation

**Game Timer**
- Time authority lives in the GameState
- UI binds to a replicated Timer ViewModel

### Why This Works

✅ Widgets are stateless and disposable
✅ ViewModels are reusable and context-aware
✅ Gameplay systems evolve without touching UI
✅ Multiplayer-safe and scalable
✅ Layout changes don't require refactoring logic

mechanics.title: Character Selector Screen
mechanics.description:
Implemented a character selector using a state-driven MVVM approach to keep UI logic deterministic, scalable, and decoupled from rendering.

### Technical Architecture

**Data-Driven Foundation**
- Character definitions live in a data table
- Data is ingested into a View Model that owns all UI-relevant state
- UI widgets bind to the View Model and update via data change notifications, not direct calls

**UI State Management**
- Hover events update the Active Character state in the View Model
- No widget-to-actor dependencies
- ViewModel manages the current selection state and exposes it through observable bindings

### Rendering & Feedback Pipeline

**Actor-Based Rendering**
- A dedicated selector actor observes View Model state changes
- Swaps skeletal meshes and triggers character-specific animations
- Writes resolved character name and ability metadata back into the View Model
- UI refreshes automatically through bindings

**Separation of Concerns**
- Rendering logic lives in the actor, not the UI
- UI drives state, actor drives visuals
- Clean propagation of data back to UI creates a full feedback loop

### Interaction Polish

**Responsive Spatial Feedback**
- Mouse-delta driven rotation adds lightweight spatial feedback
- Keeps character presentation reactive without polluting UI code with transform logic
- Rotation state is managed by the selector actor independently

### Why This Approach Matters

✅ Clear ownership of state (ViewModel owns truth)
✅ Predictable UI updates through data bindings
✅ Easy extensibility when adding new characters or views
✅ UI logic remains testable and maintainable
✅ Actor rendering can evolve without UI changes
✅ Multiplayer-ready through replicated ViewModel data

mechanics.title: Ability Upgrade and Stacking
mechanics.description:
I've been iterating on my Ability System + UI pipeline, taking cues from the high-readability design found in Deadlock. The goal: total decoupling and 100% data-driven feedback.

The backbone of this setup is a robust ViewModel architecture that serves as the authoritative bridge between gameplay logic and the HUD.

### System-Level Highlights

🔹 **Unified ViewModel Pattern**
Both the gameplay logic and the UI consume a single ViewModel. By exposing metadata, level state, and scaling values in one place, I've eliminated "UI drift." When the underlying data changes, the UI reacts no manual refreshing required.

🔹 **Tag-Driven Stacking Mechanics**
I've extended the base ability class to support stack-based progression (e.g., on-kill buffs). By using Gameplay Tags to define stacking rules, the system remains generic and reusable. This allows me to plug stacking behavior into any new ability without writing unique code.

🔹 **Conditional UI Rendering**
The UI is now context-aware. The ViewModel evaluates if an ability implements a stacking interface or exposes specific tags. If it does, the stack counter renders; if not, it stays hidden. This keeps the HUD clean and prevents "hard-coded bloat."

🔹 **Live Instance Scaling (No Re-Granting)**
Perhaps the most important technical win: scaling now mutates the existing granted ability instance. By avoiding the "remove and regrant" cycle, I ensure that active cooldowns, ongoing effects, and network states remain completely intact during a level-up or stack update.

### The Result

A system where adding a complex, multi-tiered ability takes minutes instead of hours, because the framework handles the heavy lifting of state propagation and visual feedback automatically.
